newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo aluminium futures off to slow start.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo aluminium futures off to slow start.

text.p: The first week of trading in Tokyo Commodity Exchange (TOCOM) aluminium futures was quieter than expected, due partly to a lack of participation by the local aluminium industry, market and industry sources said.
Local traders also complained that arbitrage opportunities were limited by the contract's low level of liquidity.
"We're checking TOCOM prices every day, but we have no plan to trade there," a senior official at a major Japanese aluminium fabricator said.
"We've been trading on the LME (London Metal Exchange) and have no problems at the moment. Why do we need another contract?" he said.
A senior trader at a major Japanese trade house added that orders from the local aluminium industry would be needed to boost volume on TOCOM.
"We're interested in arbitrage and are watching both markets (LME and TOCOM), but the current liquidity is lower than we expected," he said.

Trading volume on Monday, when the aluminium futures made their debut, was relatively brisk at 19,645 lots, but market sources said this consisted mainly of so-called "congratulatory orders" from local trade houses and commodity brokers.
A slump in TOCOM prices that day also triggered active aluminium selling by some investment funds in London and New York, traders said.
Turnover trailed off in the following days, however, falling to 8,290 lots on Tuesday, 5,334 on Wednesday and 8,897 on Thursday. Open interest as of Thursday was 18,704 lots.
Prices have moved largely in line with the LME and yen/dollar exchange rates.
On Friday the TOCOM benchmark February 1998 contract closed down 0.9 yen at 208.1 yen per kg, compared with a three-month LME quote at that time of about $1,590 a tonne, or 200 yen a kg.
TOCOM officials downplayed the aluminium contract's slow start.
"As we gain sufficient liquidity and influence, new participants will join," TOCOM president Naozo Mabuchi said.
"If traders want arbitrage opportunities between the Tokyo and London markets, we may consider extending the trading time," he added.
TOCOM officials said they compiled their budget for this year based on the assumption of daily aluminium futures turnover of about 15,000 lots.
The contract is being traded on TOCOM's automated trading system, along with precious-metal contracts.
Japan's aluminium industry has consistently voiced strong opposition to the new TOCOM contract.

Japan Aluminium Federation chairman Masahiro Kumamoto said in a statement earlier this week that the federation would ask TOCOM to suspend trading in the contract if its price moves too far out of line with the LME and if it damages Japan's physical market.
